title: Hispanic Heritage Month Resources, Rated
author: RatedEd
summary: RatedEd reviews the crop of Hispanic Heritage Month teaching resources that circulate every September, arguing the real quality signal isn't content but authorship — whether a resource was built by people from the community it depicts. The piece rates specific providers (Colorín Colorado, the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Latino, Library of Congress, Learning for Justice, PBS LearningMedia, publisher booklists) with concrete pros, cons, and star verdicts, and offers a fast heuristic for vetting children's books: check for the Pura Belpré, Américas, or Tomás Rivera awards. Its sharpest argument is against coloring-page-and-flag treatments of heritage months generally: reducing a culture to craft projects teaches students from that culture their heritage is decoration, an effect that lands hardest on exactly the kids the month is meant to honor. The review closes by urging teachers to integrate these books into the regular yearlong rotation rather than confining them to a September display.
points: The fastest authenticity check for children's books is award-based: Pura Belpré, Américas, and Tomás Rivera awards each signal a book made by or centering the culture it depicts.
Coloring pages and craft bundles, used as a whole unit, teach students from that culture that their heritage is a decoration rather than a living thing.
Publisher booklists are useful for discovering new titles but weak for vetting them, since presence on the list reflects what the publisher sells.
Reading a book about a Latino family in the normal February rotation communicates 'these stories are ours' in a way a themed September display cannot.
Heritage-month teaching this year intersects with real fear in immigrant communities; the review flags NEA guidance on school safe zones as worth knowing before a crisis, not during one.
quotes: Here is the problem with the forwarded lists. They are assembled by keyword. Somebody searched, grabbed twenty links, and published.
We rated for one thing above all others: who made this, and are they from the community it depicts. That is not a political standard. It is a quality standard.
If a title on a forwarded list has one of these, you can stop evaluating. If a whole list has none of them, that tells you something too.

Here is the honest problem. A month reduced to coloring pages, food, and flags teaches students that this culture is decoration. That lands hardest on the students in your room who are from that culture, who watch their heritage get treated as an art project for four weeks and then disappear.

A book about a Latino family read in February, as a normal book, in a normal week, because it is good, does more than the same book read in a heritage month display. The display says these stories are special. The February reading says these stories are ours.

Many educators are teaching this month in communities where families are anxious about immigration enforcement... a celebration of heritage lands differently for a student whose family is frightened, and being aware of that is part of teaching this month well.
